title: Private deployments — Day-2 operations, upgrade & rollback, and customer requirements library
author: Aisha Patel
content:
Summary

This document consolidates operational guidance for Redwood private deployments (VPC and on-prem). It covers day-2 operations, validated upgrade and rollback procedures, packaging constraints for air-gapped/on-prem customers, and a canonical customer requirements library used by Solutions and Sales to qualify deals. The intent is a single, actionable reference for SREs, Solutions Engineers, and Customer Ops during onboarding and ongoing operations.

Audience
- SRE and Platform engineers executing runbooks
- Solutions and Professional Services during customer on‑boarding
- Customer Ops and Site Reliability contacts at customers

Owner & Contacts
- Owner team: engineering (eng-private-deployments)
- Primary owner: Aisha Patel (eng-private-deployments)
- Backup: Liam Chen (eng-sre)

Table of contents
1) Pre-requisites and supported platforms
2) Reference architectures (VPC and on-prem)
3) Packaging and air-gap considerations
4) Day-2 operations: monitoring, backups, scaling, common tasks
5) Upgrade procedure (canary and rolling updates)
6) Rollback procedure (fast and safe rollback)
7) Customer requirements library (network, security, capacity, compliance)
8) Troubleshooting & runbook links

1) Pre-requisites and supported platforms
- Supported Kubernetes: upstream Kubernetes 1.24 - 1.27 (tested). For on-prem non-K8s installs, see the onprem-packaging guide.
- Minimum cluster capacity for production: 3 control-plane nodes + GPU worker nodes sized per workload (see capacity table below).
- Network: private subnets with NAT egress or a dedicated egress gateway; outbound HTTPS to Redwood control plane optional for managed control plane deployments.
- Required ports between customer network and components: see the Reference architecture sections.

Quick capacity table (example)
| Deployment tier | Min GPU (p4d-equivalent) | Min CPU (control-plane) | Typical memory | Notes |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | --- |
| dev / evaluation | 0.5 GPU | 2 vCPU | 16 GB | single small runtime replica |
| standard production | 2 GPUs | 4 vCPU | 32 GB | multi-replica, autoscaling configured |
| high-throughput | 8+ GPUs | 8 vCPU | 64+ GB | dedicated pools, batching enabled |

2) Reference architectures
- VPC (cloud-hosted private deployment)
  - Components: redwood-control-plane (customer-managed control-plane/optional managed control-plane), redwood-runtime (inference nodes), redwood-operator (K8s operator for lifecycle), redis/kafka (optional caching/queue), object-store for artifacts (S3-compatible).
  - Network layout: public bastion (optional) -> management subnets -> private runtime subnets -> egress NAT or proxy. CIDR requirements: provide at least /24 for control-plane + /22 for runtime pool for medium deployments.
  - Security: recommend private endpoints (no public internet facing API), customer KMS integration for secrets, and private peering between Redwood managed services and customer VPC where applicable.

- On-prem reference (air-gapped or customer datacenter)
  - Pattern: control-plane (customer-managed) installed into customer Kubernetes cluster or OpenShift. Runtime nodes on GPU hosts behind private network.
  - Artifact delivery: offline bundle (OCI images + Helm charts) delivered via secure artifact repository. Provide checksums and signed manifests.
  - Optional components: hardware HSM integration, local metrics/observability stack (Prometheus+Grafana), and NFS/CEPH for object storage.

3) Packaging & on-prem considerations
- Packaging artifacts shipped as: release tarball (signed), Helm chart tarball, and an OCI image bundle for air-gapped registries.
- Signing: all releases are GPG signed. Operator and control-plane images have immutable tags and signed manifests.
- Required artifacts for install: 
  - redwood-operator:vX.Y.Z (OCI)
  - redwood-control-plane:vX.Y.Z (OCI)
  - redwood-runtime:vX.Y.Z (OCI)
  - helm-chart-redwood-X.Y.Z.tgz
  - upgrade-manifest-X.Y.Z.json (checksums + migration steps)

Air-gap install checklist (high level)
1. Customer provides internal registry credentials and accepts signed manifests.
2. Upload OCI images to internal registry.
3. Load Helm charts and manifests into local artifact storage.
4. Run install script with --airgap flag; operator validates checksums and verifies signatures.

Example install command (air-gapped):

./install.sh --helm-chart ./helm-chart-redwood-1.6.0.tgz --oci-registry myregistry.internal:5000 --airgap \
  --control-plane-replicas 3 --runtime-node-selector "gpu=true"

4) Day-2 operations
A. Monitoring & Alerting (what to watch)
- Key health metrics:
  - control_plane_api_error_rate > 1% over 5m -> P1
  - runtime_cpu_utilization > 85% sustained 10m -> P2
  - gpu_mem_utilization > 90% sustained 5m -> P1
  - request_tail_latency_p99 > 3s -> P1
- Recommended dashboards: per-cluster model invocation latency, token throughput, per-model token cost estimates, and per-node GPU utilization. Use Prometheus + Grafana or the customer observability stack.
- Alerting rules example:
  - alert: RuntimeHighGPUUsage
    expr: avg_over_time(gpu_mem_utilization[5m]) > 0.9
    for: 5m
    labels: {severity: "page"}

B. Backups and recovery
- Objects to back up:
  - control-plane DB (Postgres) daily snapshot; retention: 30 days
  - operator CRDs exported daily (kubectl get crd -o yaml)
  - model artifact registry metadata and checksums (S3 snapshot)
- Restore cadence tested quarterly in staging.

C. Scaling & capacity management
1. Horizontal autoscaling: horizontal pod autoscaler for control-plane components with CPU and custom metrics (invocations/sec).
2. Vertical scaling for runtime: prefer adding GPU nodes; guide customers to increase worker pool size rather than vertically scaling single nodes.
3. Batching and KV cache: enable automatic batching and prefix caching per workload to reduce required GPUs by up to 2x for many workloads.

D. Common day-2 procedures (step-by-step)
- Add a new model artifact to runtime:
  1. Upload model artifacts to customer S3-compatible storage with correct path and checksum.
  2. Create a Model CRD describing the model version and resource hints (example snippet below).
  3. Operator will pull the artifact and create runtime replicas; monitor pod creation and logs.

Model CRD example (simplified):
apiVersion: redwood.ai/v1
kind: Model
metadata:
  name: llama-2-13b-v1
spec:
  artifactPath: s3://redwood-models/llama-2-13b/v1
  resources:
    gpu: 1
    memory: 128Gi

- Rotate TLS certificates (recommended every 90 days): use the control-plane CLI or cert rotation playbook in runbooks/rotate-certs.

5) Upgrade procedure (canary + rolling)
Goals: zero data loss, minimal latency impact, ability to abort to previous version.
Pre-upgrade checklist:
- Backup Postgres snapshot and export CRDs (see Backups above).
- Verify all cluster nodes are Ready and no outstanding critical alerts.
- Confirm artifact checksums and signatures on the upgrade manifest.
- Announce maintenance windows to customer stakeholders if changes are disruptive.

Canary upgrade (recommended for major versions):
1. Deploy control-plane vX.Y.Z to a single canary replica in a dedicated namespace (control-plane-canary).
2. Route 1–5% of production traffic to the canary using the router policy (example: weighted routing at the edge).
3. Monitor key metrics for 30–60 minutes: API error rates, invocation latency, cache hit-rate, memory/GPU usage.
4. If no regressions, incrementally increase traffic (10%, 25%, 50%) with monitoring windows.
5. Promote canary to full rollout using the operator: a rolling update across control-plane replicas, followed by runtime image rollouts.

Rolling update (minor/patch releases):
1. Patch operator and control-plane images via Helm: helm upgrade redwood ./helm-chart -f values-production.yaml --set image.tag=vX.Y.Z --timeout 10m
2. Wait for control-plane pods to become Ready.
3. Sequentially update runtime pools per availability zone, verifying readiness and model serving functionality after each zone.
4. Validate throughput and latency after update; if regressions occur, execute rollback procedure.

Validation checks after upgrade:
- smoke test: run a predefined prompt set and validate outputs against golden responses (automated regression harness).
- load test: submit a short synthetic traffic spike to validate autoscaling and batching.
- observability check: ensure dashboards report normal ranges and no new critical alerts.

6) Rollback procedure (fast safe rollback)
When to rollback:
- P99 latency increases by >50% or API error-rate increases >2% sustained for 5m post-upgrade
- Unrecoverable PodCrashLoop or OOMs across runtime nodes

Fast rollback steps (recommended):
1. Abort traffic to the new version: switch router weights to previous stable version (edge/router change).
2. Run helm rollback: helm rollback redwood <previous-revision> --namespace redwood --timeout 5m
3. If runtime images were changed, redeploy previous runtime image tag across runtime pools: kubectl set image deployment/runtime-xyz runtime=redwood/runtime:vX.Y.Z-previous -n redwood
4. Monitor health for 10–15 minutes. If stable, run post-rollback validation (smoke tests).

Safe rollback for stateful migrations (if DB migrations were applied)
- If upgrade included immutable DB migrations, rollback may require restoring Postgres snapshot taken pre-upgrade. Follow restore playbook:
  1. Put system in maintenance mode (stop accepting writes where feasible).
  2. Restore Postgres snapshot to a staging DB and run data-consistency checks.
  3. Point control-plane to restored DB endpoint and verify service health before accepting traffic.

7) Customer requirements library (canonical checklist)
Use this checklist during qualification and SOW drafting. Each line is a common customer ask or requirement and recommended Redwood guidance.
- Network connectivity:
  - Requirement: Private VPC peering and no public endpoints.
    Guidance: Support private endpoints; provide VPC peering instructions and required CIDR ranges.
- Data residency:
  - Requirement: Data must remain in-region.
    Guidance: Deploy control-plane and runtime in customer's target region; confirm S3/OCI registry placement.
- Security & compliance:
  - Requirement: KMS/HSM integration, audit logs, RBAC.
    Guidance: We support KMS integrations (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault) and provide audit log export via fluentd.
- Observability:
  - Requirement: Prometheus metrics and Grafana dashboards accessible to customer.
    Guidance: Export metrics using Prometheus remote write; provide Grafana templates.
- Throughput targets:
  - Requirement: 100k tokens/sec peak with P99 < 300ms for classification workloads.
    Guidance: Validate in performance ramp; recommend dedicated GPU pools and batching settings.
- Patch/upgrade windows:
  - Requirement: Non-disruptive upgrades during business hours.
    Guidance: Use canary + rolling upgrades; define maintenance windows in SOW.
- Air-gap/air-gapped:
  - Requirement: Fully offline installation.
    Guidance: Provide signed OCI bundle with install scripts and offline verification.

8) Troubleshooting & runbook links
- Runbooks (short list):
  - runbooks/rotate-certs (TLS rotation)
  - runbooks/restore-postgres (DB restore procedure)
  - runbooks/scale-runtime (add GPU nodes safely)
  - runbooks/incident-response (pager escalation)

Common diagnostic commands
- Check operator status: kubectl -n redwood get deployments -l app=redwood-operator
- Export CRDs: kubectl get models,deployments,serving -o yaml > /tmp/redwood-crds.yaml
- Tail logs for a failing runtime pod: kubectl logs -n redwood <pod-name> -c runtime --follow

Appendix: Example smoke test script
1. curl -X POST https://<private-endpoint>/v1/generate -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"model": "gpt-lite-1", "prompt":"Say hello"}'
2. Verify response status 200 and output contains expected tokens.
3. Run result diff against golden output stored in S3.
